metadata.grounding_note: Questions emphasize practical blockchain infrastructure, custody and abstraction tradeoffs, selective fit, provenance, and real-world implementation risks while avoiding brand, date, and report-metadata trivia.

lectures.title: Blockchain in the Real World - lesson slides
Blockchain in the Real World - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A user clicks a button in a dApp to swap tokens and assumes they are interacting directly with the blockchain itself. What is the best correction to that assumption?
questions.correct_answer: The user is interacting through interface and infrastructure layers that translate intent into signed transactions and chain queries.
incorrect_answers: The user is bypassing the entire standard node network that sends local transaction state directly to decentralized ledger storage.
The user is operating through local client databases that mirror standard transaction updates before blocks are produced on-chain.
The user is generating a block on local client hardware that relays final consensus states directly to the peer validating nodes.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames real blockchain use as mediated by wallets, dApps, exchanges, RPC providers, indexers, and other abstractions. These layers shape what the user can do and where risks or failures can appear.

questions.question_stem: Which sequence best describes how a simple wallet action becomes accepted blockchain state?
questions.correct_answer: The wallet creates and signs a transaction, infrastructure broadcasts it to nodes, nodes validate and propagate it, and block producers order it into the ledger under consensus rules.
incorrect_answers: The interface logs the application intent, indexers send it to validators, validators sign the user's private keys, and the external databases sync the changes under protocol rules.
The wallet sends an unsigned client message, oracle networks broadcast it to providers, providers authorize it, and gateways commit it into the ledger under standard database APIs.
The dApp holds the user's action, bridge software relays it to sidechains, sidechains batch it, and settlement nodes copy it into the base layer under optional network agreements.
questions.explanation: The transaction pipeline runs from user intent to wallet signing, RPC or node broadcast, validation and propagation, block production, and eventual accepted state. Each layer has a distinct role.

questions.question_stem: A learner says, "My wallet stores my coins, so losing the wallet file deletes the assets from the blockchain." Which response best matches the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: A wallet manages keys and signs transactions; assets are recorded on the ledger, but losing key access can make them unusable.
incorrect_answers: A wallet stores coins and balances locally on the user's device; physical tokens remain on its drive, so losing storage deletes them.
A wallet downloads blocks and saves ledger copies for each account; backup is kept on a local node, so syncing errors reset assets.
A wallet functions as a bank account interface; keys are issued by the central network, so losing access has no effect on movement.
questions.explanation: Wallets are control layers, not containers of coins. They manage private keys and authorize actions over ledger-recorded assets, so compromise, loss, or mistaken signing affects control.

questions.question_stem: A newcomer wants easy password recovery and customer support, while an experienced user wants direct control with no platform able to freeze access. Which comparison best captures the custody tradeoff?
questions.correct_answer: Custodial services improve convenience and recovery by delegating key control, while self-custody increases autonomy but makes key loss and signing mistakes more severe.
incorrect_answers: Custodial services improve safety by eliminating third-party platform risks, while self-custody reduces platform risks but makes keys harder to recover safely.
Self-custody setups limit platform and governance risk by keeping the keys private, while custodial wallets prevent hacking but guarantee protection against key loss.
Custodial systems deliver equal control by standardizing interfaces, while self-custody provides key autonomy but requires operational management of private keys.
questions.explanation: The lesson avoids ranking custody models as universally safe or unsafe. Custody choices move control, recovery options, platform dependence, and irreversible responsibility to different places.

questions.question_stem: A popular wallet app depends on a single RPC provider. During an outage, users cannot see balances or submit transactions through the app even though the blockchain network is still producing blocks. What does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: RPC providers make node access usable, but dependence on them can become an availability and visibility chokepoint.
incorrect_answers: RPC providers execute chain consensus, so provider failure can halt validator block production and network finality.
RPC providers manage wallet private keys, so disconnection can cause permanent signing-key loss and account depletion.
RPC providers act as canonical ledgers, so dependence on them can rewrite balances during application outages and forks.
questions.explanation: Apps often use RPC infrastructure rather than running their own node access stack. That improves usability but can concentrate dependence for reads, transaction submission, and user perception of network availability.

questions.question_stem: In a blockchain network, why is it misleading to say that nodes and validators always do the same job?
questions.correct_answer: Nodes verify, store, and relay network state, while validators or miners are responsible for ordering transactions into blocks under the consensus process.
incorrect_answers: Nodes construct, display, and manage wallet interfaces for users, while validators or miners hold private keys and restore accounts through recovery services.
Nodes aggregate, publish, and distribute oracle data feeds to contracts, while validators or miners transform user queries through indexing pipelines directly.
Nodes lock, escrow, and release assets across separate chains, while validators or miners set wrapped-token market prices under general bridge governance rules.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes maintaining and checking state from producing blocks and participating in ordering. Honest nodes can still validate rules even when they are not block producers.

questions.question_stem: A lending smart contract liquidates positions when an on-chain price feed reports a sharp price drop, but the feed was delayed and did not reflect the current market. Which lesson concept best explains the failure mode?
questions.correct_answer: Oracles connect smart contracts to external information, so their reporting, aggregation, update timing, and dispute design can directly affect contract outcomes.
incorrect_answers: Indexers compile smart contracts into database formats, so their indexing, tables, dashboard views, and local query pipelines can directly affect settlement balances.
Bridges transfer smart contracts to independent chains, so their wrapping, relays, liquidity pools, and custody signatures can directly affect token valuations.
Layer 2s settle smart contracts on secondary pathways, so their batching, sequencers, fraud proofs, and dispute delays can directly affect execution outcomes.
questions.explanation: Deterministic smart contracts cannot simply query the web. They depend on oracle mechanisms for external data, and stale or manipulated oracle inputs can cause incorrect on-chain behavior.

questions.question_stem: A portfolio dashboard shows a user's historical token transfers instantly, but one displayed transfer is missing because the dashboard's data pipeline is behind. What should students infer about indexers from this scenario?
questions.correct_answer: Indexers make chain data searchable and application-friendly, but they are derived read infrastructure rather than the canonical ledger.
incorrect_answers: Indexers validate consensus states as correct and final, but they are primary validator systems rather than the secondary display software.
Indexers store private keys securely and automatically, but they are local signing components rather than the public blockchain nodes.
Indexers lock native assets securely and cross-chain, but they are external bridge tools rather than the underlying network ledgers.
questions.explanation: Raw blockchain data is not optimized for fast application queries. Indexers transform blocks, logs, and events into usable views, but the chain remains the source of canonical state.

questions.question_stem: A user bridges an asset from Chain A to Chain B. The interface says the asset has moved, but the mechanism actually locks assets on Chain A and issues a linked representation on Chain B. What is the main lesson takeaway?
questions.correct_answer: Bridges enable cross-chain use by adding lock, relay, verification, mint, or release mechanisms, which also introduce additional trust and security assumptions.
incorrect_answers: Bridges execute physical transfer processes by transporting standard native tokens across ledgers, which will also eliminate external custody and validation risks.
Bridges maintain simple indexer interfaces by displaying past event, balance, or history logs, which also exclude critical consensus and smart-contract risks.
Bridges prevent asset fragmentation by standardizing native, wrapped, and synthetic tokens, which also deliver perfect economic and price parity guarantees.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that separate blockchains do not natively share state. Bridge designs can improve interoperability, but wrapped or linked assets add validation, custody, liquidity, and failure risks.

questions.question_stem: A city department proposes using blockchain for an internal database controlled by one office, with no need for public auditability or coordination across independent parties. How should the proposal be evaluated using the lesson's fit criteria?
questions.correct_answer: It is a weak fit unless blockchain properties solve a real coordination, auditability, or limited-trust problem that a simpler database cannot address.
incorrect_answers: It is a strong fit because the blockchain protocols deliver an absolute storage, transaction, or database solution that standard servers cannot replicate.
It is a strong fit provided that the department deploys a native utility, governance, or payment token that external network auditors cannot inspect.
It is an impossible evaluation until agencies measure the speculative, financial, or trading price that cryptocurrency markets can never stabilize.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents blockchain value as selective. The costs and dependencies are more defensible when multiple parties need shared state, auditability, or reduced reliance on a single operator.

questions.question_stem: A pharmaceutical supply chain involves manufacturers, shippers, pharmacies, and regulators that need to trace a drug batch across organizational boundaries. Why might the CRS reading treat this as a plausible blockchain provenance use case?
questions.correct_answer: Multiple parties need a shared, auditable history of origin and handoffs without relying entirely on one recordkeeper.
incorrect_answers: Several government regulators require a completely secret logistics system without depending directly on legal protocols.
Participating firms eliminate a manual, standardized database setup without coordinating actively on standard rules.
Enterprise supply chains demand a public, decentralized routing structure without relying on permissioned parties.
questions.explanation: The reading frames provenance as knowing an item's origin and history. Blockchain may help when goods, credentials, rights, or assets move across parties that need shared records and limited trust in a single operator.

questions.question_stem: A farm uploads a false origin record to a supply-chain blockchain, and the record later becomes difficult to alter. What does the reading say this scenario reveals?
questions.correct_answer: Tamper-resistant records can make later changes detectable, but they do not guarantee that the original off-chain data was truthful.
incorrect_answers: Automated consensus audits can inspect physical farm events directly, so they fully guarantee the submitted origin data is authentic.
Immutable ledger entries can make historical disputes replaceable, but they do not guarantee that the corrected state is accurate.
Distributed node validators can make physical records unalterable, but they do not guarantee that the cargo route was compliant.
questions.explanation: The reading repeatedly distinguishes auditability from data quality. Hashing and replication can protect the record after entry, but trustworthy provenance still depends on data capture, verification, standards, and participant behavior.

questions.question_stem: A government credential system needs known issuers, selective visibility, efficient validation, and privacy controls rather than open anonymous participation. Which design lesson from the CRS reading best applies?
questions.correct_answer: A permissioned or consortium blockchain may fit better because real deployments often need controlled read, submit, or validate rights.
incorrect_answers: A public or permissionless blockchain may perform better because open networks often require centralized read, submit, or validate rights.
A private or single-node chain may scale better because centralized systems often guarantee absolute read, submit, or validate rules.
A standard client-server database is identical to a consortium blockchain because local tables automatically create shared provenance.
questions.explanation: The reading separates public/private from permissioned/permissionless dimensions and notes that enterprise, government, identity, and supply-chain systems may need known validators, access control, privacy, and governance.
